title: Rethinking Joint Maximum Mean Discrepancy for Visual Domain Adaptation

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof asserts that "K^2 ⊙ M^J = M^{C,c}" and "K^3 ⊙ M^J = M^{WC,c}." This is false as written: K^2 and K^3 have nonzero blocks for every class c, whereas M^{C,c} and M^{WC,c} are each the matrix for one particular class. The correct relation is K^2 ⊙ M^J = sum_c M^{C,c}, and similarly K^3 ⊙ M^J = sum_c M^{WC,c}. The stated equality invalidates the proof of the claimed unification theorem.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.2, definition of K^1 in Theorem 1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper says "K^1 = I_{n×n} is a matrix whose elements are all 1." The identity matrix does not have all entries equal to one. This matters materially: I ⊙ M^J retains only the diagonal of M^J and is not the marginal-MMD matrix. The Appendix instead defines K^1=1_{n×n}, which is the form needed for the claimed MMD special case; the main theorem must be corrected.

K^{YY} is introduced as a label kernel k^Y(y_i,y_j), induced by a mapping phi(y). However, K^2, K^3, and K^4 are not functions of labels alone: their values depend on whether samples are in source versus target, on domain-specific class counts n^{s,c},n^{t,c}, and on sample membership in D^{s,c}/D^{t,c}. Thus they cannot be the stated label kernel k^Y(y_i,y_j) without redefining the kernel input to include domain/sample-dependent information. Showing that a particular finite matrix is PSD does not repair the inconsistency with the claimed label-only RKHS mapping.

predicted_errors.error_location: Sections 3.2–3.3 and experimental claims involving soft labels
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The method formally allows probability soft labels, but K^2, K^3, and K^4 are defined by hard predicates such as x_i in D^{s,c} and class counts n^{s,c}. No definition is provided for these predicates or counts under soft labels. Nevertheless, the experiments explicitly report results using "Soft" labels (Table 5). Hence the kernel used for soft-label experiments is unspecified and the method as written cannot be reproduced for that setting.

The paper calls tr(K^{XX}(K^{YY}⊙M^H)) "HSIC" but never defines M^H. More fundamentally, standard HSIC is the squared Hilbert--Schmidt norm of a centered cross-covariance operator, with an empirical form involving centering matrices (e.g., tr(KHLH), up to normalization). The paper explicitly defines and uses an uncentered feature-label cross-moment/covariance, then labels its unspecified expression HSIC. Without M^H and its centering/normalization, Eq. (4) neither defines a reproducible loss nor establishes that it is HSIC as attributed to Gretton et al. [26].

For a symmetric weight matrix W and Laplacian L=D-W, the standard identity is sum_{i,j} w_{ij}||z_i-z_j||^2 = 2 tr(ZLZ^T), not tr(ZLZ^T) as Eq. (6) states. Eq. (8) repeats the same claimed exact rewriting. The missing factor of two does not generally change an unconstrained minimizer by itself, but the equations and claimed equality are mathematically incorrect.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix E, proof that K^4 is a reproducing kernel, Eq. (45)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Eq. (45) claims x^T G^4 x = sum_{i,j} w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2. For the Laplacian structure actually encoded by K^4, the right-hand side equals 2x^T Lx under the usual symmetric double-sum convention, not x^T Lx. Moreover, Eq. (46) defines W, whereas the proof never explicitly establishes the required G^4=L relation. The PSD conclusion may be salvageable after correcting the Laplacian argument, but the presented proof is invalid as written.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.4 and Abstract/Conclusion claims that "JMMD degrades feature discrimination"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The graph-sign argument is derived only after choosing the particular class-conditional kernel K^2. Yet Section 3.5 explicitly permits K^J=K^1, K^2, or K^3. With K^1, JMMD is marginal MMD and has no class-specific same-class weights of the asserted form. Therefore the paper does not establish the general claim that JMMD itself necessarily pushes same-class within-domain samples apart or degrades discrimination; at most it analyzes one specially selected label-kernel construction.
The six listed OGL2P+JMMD-HSIC accuracies are 96.1, 95.3, 77.6, 98.1, 77.1, and 99.1. Their arithmetic mean is 90.55%, which rounds to 90.6%, not the reported 90.1%.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.2 claims about OGL2P+JMMD-HSIC on Office-31 versus Table 1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text says OGL2P+JMMD-HSIC improves over OGL2P and "achieves the best average results among all compared approaches," with a 0.3% gain over RSDA-MSTN. Table 1 instead reports OGL2P+JMMD-HSIC as 90.1% (or 90.6% after correcting its arithmetic), below OGL2P at 90.7% and well below RSDA-MSTN at 91.2%. Thus the stated improvement and best-method conclusion are false for the displayed Office-31 results.

Both tables describe Office-31 averages with ResNet-50 features and the same OGL2P/OGLP baseline plus JMMD-HSIC. Table 1 reports 90.1% for OGL2P+JMMD-HSIC, while Table 3 reports 91.5% for OGLP+JMMD-HSIC. The paper provides no different protocol, seed aggregation, or hyperparameter setting that could explain the 1.4-point discrepancy.

The text says that on D1 and D2, OGL2P+JMMD-HSIC improves over OGL2P by 0.4%/0.7% and achieves the best average result. Table 6 contradicts this for D1: OGL2P is 94.6%, while OGL2P+Our is 94.3%, a 0.3-point decline. Consequently it is neither an improvement nor the best result in that table.

The paper says that delta was "targeted manual tun[ed] per dataset to maximize performance, with selective reporting of best results" for two variants, but provides no held-out source validation protocol, unlabeled criterion, search grid, or indication that target test labels were not used. Selecting and selectively reporting the best setting per benchmark invalidates a fair comparison unless a validation protocol is specified. This is especially problematic because the claimed gains are often below one percentage point.

The paper describes ImageCLEF-DA as "a constructed dataset synthesized for this study." ImageCLEF-DA is an established public domain-adaptation benchmark, commonly consisting of the Caltech-256, ImageNet ILSVRC 2012, and Pascal VOC 2012 domains, not a dataset constructed by this paper. The paper also gives no appropriate citation for the benchmark while misrepresenting its provenance.
